To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“Abandoned croplands in Central and Eastern Europe can be restored by spontaneous grassland recovery or by active grassland restoration.

(1) the restoration of grassland biodiversity and ecosystem services on abandoned croplands can contribute to the goals of nature conservation and sustainable agriculture; (2) active grassland restoration can be a cost‐effective strategy for suppressing noxious weeds, but the spontaneous recovery of grassland biodiversity is also a viable solution; (3) the spontaneous recovery of biodiversity and active grassland restoration are mutually exclusive; and (4) the success of both restoration methods depends on the initial soil seed bank, and

(i) grassland restoration on former arable lands is an effective way to recover biodiversity and ecosystem functions, (ii) spontaneous grassland recovery and sowing are equally effective in terms of biodiversity recovery and ecosystem service provision, (iii) spontaneous grassland restoration is a cost‐effective way to restore biodiversity and ecosystem functions on croplands.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential of spontaneous and active grassland restoration as an alternative for the management of abandoned croplands in Central‐and Eastern Europe.
the question whether grassland restoration on former agricultural fields can be a viable solution for both nature conservation and agriculture.

the potential for the restoration of grassland biodiversity and ecosystem services on abandoned croplands in Central and Eastern Europe, and the role of spontaneous grassland succession vs. active restoration by seed sown in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
grassland restoration is an effective strategy for the recovery of abandoned croplands.
grassland restoration can be a win‐win solution for agriculture and nature conservation, but it requires careful planning and management to be successful.
spontaneous grassland recovery is a good strategy for biodiversity conservation, but seed sowing is a good strategy to suppress weeds and to increase biomass production.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the abandonment of cropland offers a great opportunity to restore grasslands in Central‐ and Eastern European agricultural landscapes, and that both spontaneous and active grassland restoration can be cost‐efficient and/or profitable.
the restoration of grassland on abandoned croplands is a win‐win strategy, as it can be beneficial both for nature conservation and agriculture.

spontaneous grassland recovery can be the most cost‐effective method for restoring biodiversity and weed control, while active restoration by seed sowning is the most cost‐efficient for weed control and biomass harvest.
The main takeaway from our work is that

spontaneous recovery and active grassland restoration can be complementary strategies for the recovery of biodiversity, weed suppression, biomass production and ecosystem services on former cropland sites.

grassland restoration can be an effective and cost‐effective strategy for suppressing weeds and invasive species, supporting animal husbandry, and for recovering biodiversity and ecosystem services on abandoned croplands.
grassland restoration can be an effective solution for both nature conservation and agriculture, and it can be implemented in the short term.
